prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an important and timely problem: how a user can determine whether a black-box LLM API is actually serving the same distribution as a claimed reference model, or whether it has been altered through quantization, watermarking, finetuning, or other implementation changes. The paper formalizes this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, proposes MMD-based tests with string kernels, and empirically argues that a simple Hamming kernel is particularly effective in the low-sample regime. It then applies the method to commercial APIs serving Llama-family models and reports that a substantial fraction of endpoints appear distributionally different from Meta’s released weights.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and stronger than many purely anecdotal API auditing studies. The framing is clean, the methodology is simple enough to be adopted by practitioners, and the empirical audit of real providers is compelling. The paper’s main conceptual contribution is not a new statistical test per se, but rather the formulation of API auditing as model equality testing together with the empirical case that an appropriately chosen kernelized two-sample test is useful in this domain. I think this is a worthwhile contribution. At the same time, there are several methodological and interpretational issues that should be clarified before I would be fully convinced by the strongest claims, especially those concerning commercial providers.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation. Casting “is this API serving the same model?” as a hypothesis test over prompt-completion distributions is elegant and general. It naturally subsumes both provider-vs-reference auditing and temporal drift detection. This is a better fit than benchmark-only auditing because it directly targets the sampled distribution rather than only task accuracy under greedy decoding. I also appreciated the emphasis on user-chosen prompt distributions, which makes the framework application-specific rather than benchmark-centric.

The empirical finding that a simple Hamming kernel works well is also useful. In high-dimensional discrete spaces, universal kernels or exact-match multinomial tests can indeed be ineffective at small sample sizes, so the argument for a coarser but more sample-efficient similarity notion is plausible. The experiments comparing Hamming MMD to one-hot, all-substrings, and classical multinomial tests support this point reasonably well. The paper does a good job showing that exact-match style tests collapse when completions are long and collisions are rare. The practical sample efficiency numbers are appealing.

The real-world audit is the paper’s most attention-grabbing component, and it is valuable that the authors actually test multiple providers and models rather than stopping at simulation. The result that some endpoints appear substantially different from the reference is important if robust. The attempt to quantify effect size via estimated MMD, rather than only binary rejection, is also a strength.

That said, I have several concerns.

My main concern is about what exactly is being tested in the API audit, and how confidently one can attribute rejection to “the provider changed the model.” In practice, many factors besides weight modifications can alter the observed completion distribution: undocumented system prompts, safety filters, prompt preprocessing, tokenizer/version mismatches, decoding implementation differences, stop-sequence handling, repetition penalties, top-p defaults, semantic caching, load balancing across backend variants, and nondeterministic infrastructure behavior. The paper acknowledges some of these possibilities in spirit, but the interpretation of flagged endpoints often reads stronger than the evidence supports. Statistically, the test only establishes that the observed black-box conditional distribution differs from the chosen reference setup under the tested prompts and decoding parameters. It does not identify the cause. This distinction should be made much more explicit throughout, especially in the headline claim that certain endpoints “serve different distributions than reference weights.” That statement is technically true, but readers may over-interpret it as evidence of undisclosed model substitution or harmful degradation.

Relatedly, the reference distribution itself may not be uniquely defined. The paper uses fp32 and fp16 Hugging Face inference as nulls, which is sensible, but there are still many implementation choices in local inference that can affect outputs. For example, exact sampling behavior can depend on library version, RNG implementation, batching, KV-cache behavior, and tokenizer normalization details. If the goal is to audit equivalence to “Meta’s released weights,” the paper should discuss more carefully whether the local reference pipeline is stable and representative enough to serve as ground truth. Some sensitivity analysis over inference stacks would strengthen the claims considerably.

A second concern is the statistical calibration and decision procedure used in the provider audit. The paper says tests are conducted at level alpha = 0.01 using N = 10m samples, then repeated over ten samples, and endpoints are failed if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. This is not a standard hypothesis testing protocol, and it is not obvious what overall Type I error this induces. Repeating a level-0.01 test ten times and thresholding the empirical rejection rate is a heuristic stability criterion, but it changes the operating characteristics in a way that should be analyzed. The paper gives a validity argument for the composite null rule combining p1 and p2, but not for the additional repetition-and-majority-fail rule. Since the paper’s most consequential claims rely on this procedure, I think a more formal treatment or at least a simulation-based calibration study is necessary. As written, it is hard to know how conservative or anti-conservative the final endpoint-level decisions are.

A third issue is that the Hamming kernel is not characteristic, and the paper leans heavily on empirical effectiveness rather than theoretical guarantees. That is acceptable in principle, but the limitations deserve more emphasis. If the kernel induces a pseudometric, then there exist distinct distributions that are invisible to the test. The paper notes this, but then uses estimated Hamming MMD as an effect-size proxy and even compares distances across model families. Those comparisons are interesting, but they should be framed more cautiously. A low Hamming MMD does not imply closeness in any stronger distributional sense, and even a moderate Hamming MMD may be driven by superficial stylistic regularities rather than semantically meaningful differences. The paper partly addresses this by correlating MMD with HumanEval accuracy, but the correlation is only moderate. I would encourage the authors to avoid overclaiming that MMD magnitude corresponds to practical severity without more validation.

I also have some reservations about the prompt distributions used in simulation. The Wikipedia continuation setup with random 100-character prefixes is convenient and broad, but it is somewhat artificial relative to many real API use cases. The paper does include HumanEval and UltraChat in the provider audit, which helps, but the core kernel-selection and power comparisons are mostly on the Wikipedia task. It would strengthen the paper to show that the superiority of Hamming MMD over alternatives persists on more instruction-like and code-generation-like distributions, not just in the audit stage but in the controlled power studies as well.

The comparison baselines are reasonable but not exhaustive. Since the paper’s main empirical claim is that kernel choice matters, it would be useful to compare against stronger sequence-level distances or embedding-based tests. For example, one could imagine tests based on edit distance kernels, n-gram kernels beyond all-substrings approximations, or semantic embeddings of completions. Even if those alternatives are more expensive, a limited comparison would help establish whether Hamming is genuinely the best practical choice or simply the best among a narrow set of baselines. Similarly, there is a large literature on classifier two-sample tests and learned test statistics that might be competitive in this regime.

Another concern is the dependence on character-space comparisons when tokenizers differ or when APIs only expose decoded text. Character-space Hamming distance over long strings can be sensitive to small alignment shifts, formatting differences, whitespace normalization, or Unicode quirks. The paper pads shorter strings and compares positionwise, but if one model inserts an early newline or a different indentation pattern, the remainder of the string may incur large Hamming penalties even if the semantic content is similar. This may be acceptable if the goal is literal distributional equality of returned strings, but then the semantics of the test are narrower than “same model.” Some discussion of robustness to formatting perturbations would be helpful. An edit-distance-based kernel or alignment-aware variant might be more appropriate in character space.

On the experimental side, I would like more detail on how API sampling was controlled. The paper says it explicitly requested temperature 1, but many providers expose different subsets of decoding parameters, may clamp unsupported values, or may apply hidden defaults for top-p, penalties, or stop tokens. Were all other parameters standardized and verified? Were prompts sent in exactly the same chat template format across providers? For instruction-tuned models, chat templating differences alone can materially change outputs. This is especially important because the paper interprets failures as evidence of distributional deviation from the reference model, but mismatched prompting format could itself induce such deviations.

The paper would also benefit from clearer reporting of uncertainty in the provider audit. Table 1 presents binary pass/fail outcomes, but the underlying quantities are average rejection rates over ten runs. Showing the distribution of p-values or rejection frequencies per endpoint would help readers assess borderline cases versus robust failures. Likewise, confidence intervals on the estimated MMD effect sizes would be useful, especially when making claims that some provider deviations are as large as swapping in another model.

I found the finetuning experiment suggestive but somewhat underdeveloped. Detecting finetuning after a small number of steps is interesting, but the setup uses full finetuning on 1000 examples with a specific learning rate and evaluates on a single downstream prompt distribution. It would be useful to know how detection power varies with parameter-efficient finetuning methods, smaller data sizes, or instruction tuning that is more realistic for providers. As written, the result mainly shows that sufficiently strong finetuning is detectable, which is not surprising.

There are also some presentation issues. The paper is generally readable, but a few claims are stated too strongly relative to the evidence. For example, saying that some deviations are “quite serious” because the estimated Hamming MMD matches that between different model families is rhetorically strong given that the metric is kernel-dependent and not directly tied to user utility. Similarly, the clustering interpretation that “training data, rather than scale, determines model similarity” seems speculative based on the presented evidence. The observed clustering could reflect many factors besides training data.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has substantial merit. The problem is important, the framing is elegant, the method is simple and reproducible, and the empirical audit is novel and likely to generate useful discussion. My overall assessment is positive, though not without reservations. The paper would be significantly stronger with tighter statistical treatment of the endpoint-level decision rule, more careful causal interpretation of flagged APIs, and additional robustness analyses around prompting/inference-stack differences.

The most important revisions I would request are as follows. First, clarify throughout that the test detects distributional inequality of observed outputs under a specified prompting and decoding protocol, not necessarily weight-level modification, and discuss alternative causes of rejection in more depth. Second, analyze or empirically calibrate the full provider-audit decision procedure, including the ten repeated tests and 50% threshold, so that readers understand the actual false positive behavior. Third, provide stronger robustness checks for the reference pipeline and prompt formatting, ideally including sensitivity to inference library/version and chat template choices. Fourth, expand the controlled experiments to at least one additional prompt distribution beyond Wikipedia for kernel comparison and power analysis. Fifth, report richer endpoint-level statistics than binary pass/fail.

If these issues are addressed, I think the paper could make a meaningful contribution. In its current form, I view it as a strong and practically relevant paper with some methodological looseness around the most policy-relevant claims.

My recommendation would be a weak accept to borderline accept, depending on the conference bar and on whether the authors can convincingly address the statistical calibration and interpretation concerns in rebuttal.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper formalizes auditing black-box language model APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem called Model Equality Testing. Given samples from a reference model distribution and an API distribution over prompt-completion pairs, the authors propose using MMD-based kernel tests, with a simple Hamming string kernel over completions as the main practical choice. Through simulations on quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model substitution, they show this test has substantially better small-sample power than several baselines. They then audit 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama models and report that 11 endpoints produce distributions statistically distinguishable from Meta reference weights (allowing either fp32 or fp16 as nulls). The paper also uses estimated MMD values as effect-size measures and releases code and a large completion dataset.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: users increasingly rely on black-box LLM APIs and often assume equivalence to named reference models without verification.
Clear problem formulation as a statistically principled two-sample testing task, which unifies API faithfulness and temporal drift auditing.
Method is simple, practical, and sample-efficient; the Hamming-kernel MMD test is easy to implement and does not require log-probability access.
Empirical evaluation is broad in scope, covering quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model swaps, and real commercial APIs.
Comparison against multiple baselines (one-hot MMD, all-substrings kernel, L1, chi-squared) helps justify the proposed kernel choice.
The real-world audit of 31 endpoints is compelling and likely to be of broad interest to the community.
Open-sourcing code and a large dataset improves reproducibility and downstream utility.
The paper is generally well written, with intuitive explanations of why coarse but structured kernels can outperform universal kernels in low-sample regimes.
weaknesses: The main proposed kernel is not characteristic/universal, so failure to reject does not strongly support equality; the practical semantics of acceptance are therefore limited.

The empirical setup fixes a narrow family of prompt distributions and decoding settings, leaving uncertainty about robustness to more realistic user prompt distributions, system prompts, stop sequences, and provider-side preprocessing.

The API audit conclusions may be confounded by undocumented differences unrelated to model weights, such as tokenizer/version mismatches, prompt templating, safety filters, truncation policies, hidden system prompts, or decoding implementation differences.
The decision rule for endpoint failure (average rejection rate over ten repeated tests >= 0.5) is somewhat ad hoc and not tied to a clearly analyzed operating characteristic.

The paper emphasizes power but gives limited empirical calibration evidence for Type-I error in the exact practical settings used for API audits, especially under character-space comparisons and composite null testing.
Using Hamming similarity in character space for cross-tokenizer/provider comparisons may blur whether detected differences reflect semantic/model changes or superficial formatting differences.

The claim that some APIs are as far from the reference as entirely different models is interesting but depends heavily on the chosen pseudometric and prompt distribution, so it should be interpreted cautiously.
methodological_flaws: The composite-null testing procedure in Section 5 controls FPR only for the union null via the trivial bound P(reject)=P(p1<alpha and p2<alpha)<=P(p1<alpha)<=alpha; this is valid, but the paper does not analyze how conservative the procedure becomes under dependence between p1 and p2 or how this affects reported endpoint failures. This is not incorrect, but the practical inferential consequences are underdeveloped.

The use of simulated null samples from local reference models assumes the local implementation exactly represents the intended null distribution. Any mismatch in tokenizer handling, chat template, sampling library, RNG, or EOS behavior can induce rejection unrelated to provider-side model distortion. This is a substantial empirical validity concern for the API audit section.

Character-space Hamming MMD can be sensitive to formatting artifacts (whitespace, Unicode normalization, boilerplate, code fences, safety disclaimers). Without normalization ablations, some detected differences may reflect output post-processing rather than meaningful model-distribution changes.

The paper reports power from only 100 Monte Carlo trials in several experiments; while acceptable for rough trends, this yields nontrivial uncertainty for claims about moderate power differences between tests.

The thresholding scheme for declaring an endpoint as failed after ten repeated tests lacks a formal statistical justification. Averaging binary rejections and thresholding at 0.5 effectively defines a second-stage test whose Type-I/II properties are not analyzed.

Because the Hamming kernel is only a pseudometric, estimated distances and statements comparing API deviations to inter-model deviations can be misleading if readers interpret them as model-agnostic notions of closeness. The paper notes this caveat, but some headline interpretations still risk overclaiming.

The finetuning experiments use a single model, small datasets, and one optimizer/learning-rate configuration, so broader claims about detectability of finetuning or implications for unlearning/model editing are suggestive rather than well established.
